steps.action: Frame the long-standing debate over the origin and connectivity of the CaCl2 brines of Don Juan Pond and Lake Vanda.
steps.quote: It is also notable for having a long-standing debate as to the origin and connectivity of groundwater brines in the valley.

steps.action: Report the 1970s Dry Valleys Drilling Project borehole observations at Lake Vanda (DVDP4A) and in the North Fork (DVDP14).
steps.quote: In 1973–1974, DVDP4A penetrated 17.4 m beneath the sediment–water interface of the bottom of Lake Vanda.

steps.action: Report Cartwright et al.'s hypothesis of groundwater flowing west from Lake Vanda.
steps.quote: hypothesized the presence of a groundwater system flowing from Lake Vanda to the west

steps.action: Report that the westward-flow hypothesis was rejected from fluid potentials and from the frozen DVDP14 core.
steps.quote: They later invalidated this hypothesis based on fluid potentials measured in [...] .

steps.action: Report the DVDP13 observations at Don Juan Pond: borehole water above pond level, brine salinity, and artesian flow in 1978.
steps.quote: water flowed from the hole for 3 d as an artesian well before being shut off

steps.action: Lay out the rival sources: a confined Ferrar Dolerite aquifer fed from beneath the ice sheet (McGinnis, Harris) versus surface brine generation by deliquescence and surface discharge (Gough, Dickson).
steps.quote: the fractured and highly mineralized Ferrar Dolerite might be a confined aquifer

steps.action: Cite mixing models predicting that the salts cannot come solely from surface inputs.
steps.quote: most mixing models predict that the salts in Lake Vanda and Don Juan Pond could not have originated solely from surface inputs

steps.action: Cite the Toner et al. (2017) brine-evolution model, which excludes a purely evaporative surface origin but is equivocal on a Don Juan Pond–Lake Vanda connection.
steps.quote: the ionic ratios in Don Juan Pond could only be explained by the upwelling and evaporation of deep groundwater

steps.action: State the aim of mapping subsurface water distribution and hydrological connectivity non-destructively.
steps.quote: Our research goals were to map water distribution and hydrological connectivity

steps.action: Use the helicopter-borne TEM (AEM) system flown in 2011 and 2018 and the 2017 ground-based TEM, both characterized in the authors' earlier papers (Foley 2015, Grombacher 2021, Madsen 2022).
steps.quote: A comprehensive methodology on our 2018 AEM survey can be found in

steps.action: Invert TEM decays for resistivity with 1D forward models, using an induced-polarization forward response at Don Juan Pond.
steps.quote: Inversion is used to estimate the underlying electrical resistivity structures, consistent with observed TEM signals.

steps.action: Select three E–W flight lines along the lowest-elevation tracks and set aside N–S lines whose 3D effects violate the 1D assumption.
steps.quote: These flight lines were picked to align with the lowest-elevation tracks of Wright Valley, where one might assume brine would pool

steps.action: Check the line choice against additional higher-elevation E–W lines, which returned higher resistivities.
steps.quote: Additional E–W flight lines along higher-elevation tracks returned higher resistivity readings

steps.action: Present the inversions as resistivity cross-sections and state their resolution: cross-track footprint, depth of investigation, and no-signal gaps.
steps.quote: The depth of investigation (DOI), where the signal-to-noise ratio is too low for accurate interpretation, was several hundreds of meters in many areas.

steps.action: Read the three profiles: clear surface conductors at Lake Vanda, Don Juan Pond and Don Quixote Pond, and the Vanda resistivity-depth profile.
steps.quote: the surface conductors of Lake Vanda and Don Juan Pond are clear

steps.action: Compare the Lake Vanda resistivity profile with measured lake-water EC (Castendyk 2016) and with saline sediments in DVDP4A.
steps.quote: This is consistent with electrical conductivity (EC) of lake water in Vanda

steps.action: Explain the unexpectedly high 1 Ωm at Don Juan Pond by the auxiliaries (averaging over the top 4 m, sediment porosity, CaCl2 conductivity) rather than by an absence of brine.
steps.quote: the pond itself is only 20–30 cm deep, and the AEM inversions are averaged over the top 4 m

steps.action: Compare the 23–36 m low-resistivity layer at Don Juan Pond with the hypothesized Ferrar Dolerite aquifer.
steps.quote: This depth overlaps with the hypothesized aquifer in the Ferrar Dolerite

steps.action: Bring in the soluble-salt evidence of Toner et al. (2022) and the dolerite porosity (Harris 1981) as independent support for a dolerite–brine link.
steps.quote: This is yet another line of evidence that supports a connection between Ferrar Dolerite and Don Juan Pond brine.

steps.action: Keep regional connectivity within the Don Juan Pond basin: brine on both sides of the pond and a possible link to the VXE-6 basin via a vertical low-resistivity feature.
steps.quote: In the Don Juan Pond basin, AEM data provide evidence for regional connectivity.

steps.action: Propose that brine standing above pond level (topographic control) drove the artesian discharge at DVDP13.
steps.quote: This topographic control could be responsible for the artesian well discharge observed during the DVDP drilling.

steps.action: Test valley-wide connectivity against the profiles: no conductors east of Lake Vanda and no shallow connection west to the forks.
steps.quote: [...] our AEM survey, any valley-wide groundwater connectivity [...] .

steps.action: Reconcile the North Fork shallow brines with the frozen DVDP14 core by invoking insufficient borehole depth or spatial heterogeneity.
steps.quote: it may be that it did not extend deep enough

steps.action: Cross-check the no-signal zone SW of Line 3 with ground-based TEM, which also failed to record signal, bounding any brine there to >500 m.
steps.quote: The region between Don Juan Pond and Lake Vanda was surveyed by both airborne and ground-based TEM.

steps.action: Refine the 'follow the dolerite' idea: with westward-dipping sills but no brine-saturated dolerite at the eastern South Fork, any conduit does not follow topography.
steps.quote: If there is a dolerite conduit between the two surface waterbodies, it does not follow the surface topography.

steps.action: Compare the possible >500 m connection depth with AEM brine depths and frozen–unfrozen transitions in Taylor Valley.
steps.quote: This depth is in the range at which liquid brines were inferred in Taylor Valley from AEM

steps.action: Keep the presence of unfrozen brine-saturated regions and leave valley-wide connectivity unresolved.
steps.quote: did confirm the presence of unfrozen brine-saturated regions in the subsurface

sequences.source_document: Open discussion of preprint 10.5194/tc-2022-91 (RC1, RC2, RC3, AC1, AC2 with supplements)

steps.action: Referee asks how sampling geometry affects interpretation; the authors add the cross-track sampling width (60–70 m to several hundred m) to the paper (§2 ¶4).
steps.quote: Some of this could be addressed by mentioning the cross-track sampling width of the SkyTEM.

steps.action: Authors add the flight-line selection rationale (lowest-elevation tracks) and the supporting ground-based surveys (§2 ¶3).
steps.quote: Our flight lines were picked to align with the lowest elevation tracks of the valley

steps.action: Referee calls the treatment of surface hydrology dismissive; the authors expand the review of surface processes (Gough 2017, Dickson 2013) in §1 ¶6.
steps.quote: In a revision, our aim would be to expand the literature review of DJP hydrology and provide more references to surface processes.

steps.action: Referee questions the 'labyrinth' title; the authors keep it, arguing the word suits an unresolved maze-like system.
steps.quote: but the word labyrinth evokes a complicated maze-like network

steps.action: Referee notes that 'conduits' implies localized high permeability; the authors tighten the wording (the published abstract speaks of brine, not conduits).
steps.quote: We will be more specific in our language when refering to potential

steps.action: Referee asks what stops the Line 1 conductive zone; the authors answer in the rebuttal with a guess (dolerite to granite) not added to the paper.
steps.quote: An educated guess would say it’s changing geology (Ferrar Dolerite to granite)

steps.action: Referee points out brine standing above the pond level; the authors add the elevated-brine observation and the topographic-control explanation of the artesian discharge (§3 ¶4).
steps.quote: It’s really interesting that the low resistivity regions east and west of DJP extent up higher than the modern lake level.

steps.action: Second referee (RC3) defends the deep-groundwater interpretation against RC1; the authors keep their deep-groundwater framing without new work.
steps.quote: We agree that the aforementioned modeling studies support the deep groundwater interpretation

steps.action: Referee asks whether the data show an ice-sheet source west of Don Juan Pond; the authors add that no conclusion can be drawn there (§3 ¶5).
steps.quote: From our data we can’t draw any conclusions on the source of the brine.

steps.action: Referee links the vertical feature east of Don Juan Pond to VXE-6 pond chemistry; the authors add the VXE-6 discussion (§3 ¶3–4).
steps.quote: we agree that the pond chemistry aligns well with the AEM survey east of DJP

steps.action: Authors state the depth bound on any South Fork connection (>500 m), later added to §3 ¶5 and §4 ¶1.
steps.quote: So any connection must be deeper than our penetration depth (appox. 500 m).

steps.action: Referee cites Toner et al. (2022) on dolerite-hosted CaCl2 salts; the authors add it as a further line of evidence (§3 ¶3).
steps.quote: We will add more discussion on the potential connection between hydrogeological pathways and the Ferrar Dolerite.

steps.action: Referee suggests following the dolerite's strike and dip; the authors add the 'follow the dolerite' paragraph with the McKelvey and Webb westward dip (§3 ¶5).
steps.quote: [...] ’t say much about the subsurface geology beyond the McKelvey and Webb paper

steps.action: Referee asks whether CaCl2 conductivity behaviour explains the 1 Ωm at Don Juan Pond; the authors add the CaCl2 conductivity and porosity reasoning (§3 ¶2).
steps.quote: Correct, the conductivity of CaCl2 is greater than the conductivity of an equivalent mass of NaCl.

tree.answer: CaCl2 brines in Don Juan Pond and Lake Vanda of disputed deep or surface origin
No; subsurface brine is inferred from TEM resistivity inversion
Map subsurface water distribution and hydrological connectivity
Deep dolerite groundwater vs surface/evaporative sources; connected vs isolated basins
Not formally derived; connectivity would appear as continuous conductors within the DOI
Found: existing survey lines over natural brines, no conditions set
Partly: Vanda profile matches measured EC; ground TEM agrees in no-signal zone
Brine presence kept; Vanda–Don Juan Pond connectivity unresolved
Yes; referees supportive, revisions added geometry, surface-process and dolerite caveats

end.claim: AEM resistivity sections show unfrozen brine-saturated regions in the subsurface near Lake Vanda, Don Juan Pond and the North Fork, while any Lake Vanda–Don Juan Pond connection is not resolved within the ~500 m depth of investigation.

decisive_move.sentence: Without inverting the airborne TEM data into resistivity cross-sections, with their depth of investigation, no subsurface brine could be mapped or bounded.

gates.evidence: The surveys were flown 'in exploration of liquid water' (§0 ¶1) as part of a broader programme. Lines were chosen where brine was expected to pool (§2 ¶3), so the deep-groundwater idea shaped line selection but not acquisition as a test. Brine presence could have failed: no conductors were found east of Lake Vanda, and no-signal zones were cross-checked with ground TEM. The connectivity hypothesis was not decisively tested. Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Transient electromagnetic measurement: eddy currents and decay of the secondary magnetic field
Cole-Cole re-parameterised induced-polarization forward response (Fiandaca et al. 2018)
Electrical conductivity of aqueous CaCl2 solutions (Sun and Newman 1970, Lawrence Radiation Laboratory)

novelty_claims.quote: This study provides the first integrative overview of subsurface brines in Wright Valley using non- [...] .

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: regional connectivity within the Don Juan Pond basin and a possible link to VXE-6 (best_explanation, §3 ¶4); brine hosted in Ferrar Dolerite (best_explanation, §3 ¶3); topographic control of the artesian discharge (hypothesis only, §3 ¶4); valley-wide Lake Vanda–Don Juan Pond connectivity and an ice-sheet source (no conclusion, §3 ¶5, §4 ¶1). No inversion uncertainties, misfit statistics or alternative-inversion results are shown. The ground-based TEM data, the higher-elevation lines and the N–S lines are described but not shown. The 2011 data are mentioned but the three lines shown are from 2018. Inference: the survey was not designed as a test of the connectivity hypothesis, so the walk is an application of an inherited capability to a pre-existing question. That is why no listed composition fits: it is not capability_first (rivals predate the data), not strong_inference (no crucial test), and only partly trace_series (the headline claim is an estimate, not a best explanation). Review: minor wording changes (removing 'convincing arguments', RC1 ¶8) are not coded. Whether the authors' rebuttal promises (AC2, AC1) were all carried out is inferred by matching against the published text.

disagreements.target: Interpretation of the frozen DVDP14 core as negating groundwater flow into the North Fork (DVDP era)
disagreements.support: The AEM profiles show a shallow brine layer in the North Fork; the authors argue DVDP14 was too shallow or missed a heterogeneous brine layer.
disagreements.quote: DVDP14 did not penetrate the permafrost, and it may be that it did not extend deep enough

disagreements.target: Surface generation of Don Juan Pond brine and surface hydrology control (Gough et al. 2017; Dickson et al. 2013)
disagreements.support: Cited mixing models and Toner et al. (2017), not the paper's own data, are used to argue that the salts need a deep groundwater source.
disagreements.quote: However, most mixing models predict that the salts in Lake Vanda and Don Juan Pond could not have originated solely from surface inputs

disagreements.target: Expectation that brine follows the westward-dipping Ferrar Dolerite sills ('follow the dolerite'; McKelvey and Webb 1962)
disagreements.support: No brine-saturated dolerite appears at [...] eastern end of the South Fork transect, so any conduit does not follow surface topography.
disagreements.quote: evidence of brine-saturated dolerite is not present on the eastern end of the [...]
